prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language prose that turns memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture, with a lyric foundation in his poetry

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading colleagues' arguments. On public knowledge, Cărtărescu offers the most distinctive voice on the shortlist and the longest sustained imaginative reach. The large works Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid show formal control over very long structures: dense, patterned sentences that make memory, the body and dream into a single metaphysical project. His poetic beginnings appear to inform the prose's lyric intensity rather than sit beside it as a separate strand. He has decades of major work, and the later novels seem to extend the project rather than repeat it, which bears on the sustained-quality criterion. I weigh this as literary achievement across the oeuvre, not as reputation or readership. Adonis is a very close second for me. His case on linguistic and formal renewal is as serious as any, and the difference between us is a judgement about what can be assessed. The Arabic prosodic work is the part of his achievement most exposed to translation loss.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the metaphysical scale may outrun emotional and moral range, and that the longest volumes may blur into one another. If that is so, the sustained-quality judgement is weaker than the peak works suggest. A second reservation is that my view of the sentence-level music depends on translations of stylised Romanian prose, and the poetry is least accessible to non-Romanian readers. I cannot verify either point independently, and the committee should treat both as open.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first as the strongest case on formal and linguistic achievement. He argues that the remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth and fragmentation, together with the essays on tradition, forms a fully mature oeuvre. He also notes that the achievement lies in Arabic prosody that translation conveys only partially.
responses.response: I accept the substance of this argument. On formal and linguistic renewal within a tradition, Adonis is at least as strong as Cărtărescu, and I ranked him second for those reasons. The same translation caveat applies to my own first choice, since Cărtărescu's density is also a feature of the original that may flatten in translation. I am therefore not claiming my case is better insulated. My difference from Olsson is that Cărtărescu's achievement appears to be carried by large narrative architecture, which survives partial translation loss better than prosodic and intertextual effects do. That is a judgement about assessability under uncertainty, not about greater merit, and I would not want Adonis's case discounted for it.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for recognisable voice, sustained formal ambition and imaginative depth. She raises the concern that the later volumes may not keep the same intensity and that the scale and self-referentiality could blur individual books.
responses.response: I agree with the case and with the concern. The question of whether the later novels sustain the intensity of Blinding is the central test of this candidacy, and my own record says only that they appear to extend the project. I would add that self-referentiality is not by itself a fault in an oeuvre built as one connected cosmology. It becomes a fault only if individual books stop discovering anything new. I would want the committee to test that book by book rather than assume it either way. My coverage of the late works is limited, so I cannot settle the point myself.

responses.point: Palm ranks Anne Carson first for formal invention across classical scholarship, lyric, narrative and book-object form. She ranks Cărtărescu third and notes that the density and excess of the largest works may limit consensus and weigh against sustained quality.
responses.response: I take the point about excess seriously and have no complete answer to it. Where I differ is on Carson. Her formal invention is real, but the strongest work appears concentrated in hybrid and book-object forms whose literary standing is hard to weigh in an oeuvre assessment. That is a qualification, not a dismissal. Palm's own point about reception concentrated in Anglophone culture and about uncertain breadth suggests the same concern about whether intensity at the peak translates into sustained range. I would ask whether Carson's oeuvre is a consistent literary architecture or a series of brilliant experiments. On that test, the long-form coherence of Cărtărescu seems to me the stronger evidence, though I hold this tentatively.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Adonis first and Cărtărescu third. She finds the Adonis oeuvre complete enough to judge as a whole. For Cărtărescu she says the durability of the whole remains to be tested and that scale may not always be matched by quality.
responses.response: This is a fair distinction, and I accept that Adonis's body of work is more consolidated in its critical reception. Durability is the right criterion, but it is not settled by the length of a reception history. A body of work that is decades old and still widening, as I understand Cărtărescu's to be, can be assessed now on its established major works. I would not make 'remains to be tested' a reason to defer if the central books already carry the case.

uncertainties: How well the sentence-level density and musicality of Cărtărescu's Romanian carry into the available translations, and whether translation quality is consistent across the very long novels.
Corpus coverage: his poetry and early work are less accessible in translation than the large novels, so judgement of the whole oeuvre is partial.
Whether the late novels sustain the intensity of Blinding and Solenoid, or whether scale and self-reference begin to blur individual books.

How much of Adonis's claim lies in Arabic prosody and intertextual work that I can assess only through secondary accounts, and how that should be weighed against the more translatable narrative architecture of Cărtărescu.
How far public and political positions in the reception of Adonis can be separated from the literary assessment.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile that would require recusal. For transparency: the profile records long residence in Prague and Vienna, Central Europe essays, and a literary record on Nazism and 20th-century trauma. This is thematic proximity to Claudio Magris (B007), my alternative, and loosely to the Central and Eastern European setting of Cărtărescu. I treat my own literary practice as context, not evidence of preference, and I have no documented personal tie to any shortlisted writer.
